'''''Drosera binata''''', commonly known as the '''forked sundew''' or '''fork-leaved sundew'''. It is a large, [[perennial]] [[sundew]] [[Indigenous (ecology)|native]] to south-eastern [[Australia]] and [[New Zealand]]. The [[specific name (botany)|specific epithet]] is [[Latin]] for "having pairs", a reference to the leaves, which are [[dichotomous]]ly (sometimes twice-dichotomously) divided or forked.<ref name="Salmon">Salmon, B. 2001. ''Carnivorous Plants of New Zealand''. Ecosphere Publications.</ref> These leaves are up to {{cvt|60|cm}} long.<ref>{{cite book | last1= Turner | first1= R.J. Jr. | last2= Wasson | first2= Ernie | date= 1999 | title= Botanica | location= not given | publisher= Barnes & Noble | page= 315 | isbn= 0760716420 }}</ref>

Like all sundews, it is a [[carnivorous plant]]. It is unique among sundews in having narrow, branching leaves. It is the only species in the ''Drosera'' [[section (botany)|section]] '''''Phycopsis'''''.

== Distribution and habitat ==
''D. binata'' occurs naturally in Australia, primarily in coastal areas from [[Fraser Island]] in [[Queensland]], southwards down through [[New South Wales]] and [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] to [[Tasmania]] and the south-east corner of [[South Australia]]. The range of this species extends to New Zealand where it is common below an [[elevation]] of 1,000 metres, being found in both the [[North Island|North]] and [[South Island|South]] Islands, [[Stewart Island / Rakiura]] and farther afield on the [[Chatham Islands|Chathams]].<ref name="Salmon" /> Some populations go dormant in the winter, while others are truly tropical.

==Taxonomy and botanical history==
Plants similar to the [[biological type|type specimen]], commonly referred to as the "T-form", were first collected in 1792 by the French exploration of Australia's southern coast led by [[Bruni d'Entrecasteaux]]. The naturalist on board that expedition, [[Jacques Labillardière]], first described ''D. binata'' in his 1804 publication on the flora of Australia, ''[[Novae Hollandiae Plantarum Specimen]]''. The T-form, so named for its single leaf bifurcation spreading into a T-shape, is a robust plant from temperate zones that can grow up to {{convert|30|cm|in|0|abbr=on}} and has green foliage that becomes redder with age. This form has been described as being genetically stable.<ref name="Gilbert 1984">Gilbert, I. 1984. [http://carnivorousplants.org/cpn/articles/CPNv13n3p74_76.pdf ''Drosera binata''.] ''[[Carnivorous Plant Newsletter]]'', 13(3): 74-76.</ref><ref name="Rice 2010">Rice, B. 2010. [http://www.sarracenia.com/faq/faq5270.html Any other ''Drosera'' species.] The Carnivorous Plant FAQ v. 11.5. Retrieved 25 January 2010.</ref>

The second observed form, commonly referred to as [[variety (botany)|var.]] ''dichotoma'', is similar to the T-form, but the foliage is yellower and the leaf typically divides into four terminal leaf points, though it has been known to produce as many as eight leaf points.<ref name="Gilbert 1984" /><ref name="Rice 2010" /> It was first validly described in an 1819 volume of ''[[Rees's Cyclopædia]]'' by [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]] as ''D. dichotoma'', based on the description by [[Joseph Banks]] and [[Daniel Solander]]. This name, however, has since been reduced to [[synonym (taxonomy)|synonymy]] with ''D. binata''.<ref name="Schlauer">Schlauer, J. 2010. [http://www.omnisterra.com/bot/cp_home.cgi World Carnivorous Plant List - Nomenclatural Synopsis of Carnivorous Phanerogamous Plants] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160918161537/http://www.omnisterra.com/bot/cp_home.cgi |date=2016-09-18 }}. Retrieved 25 January 2010.</ref><ref name="IPNI">{{IPNI|id=321826-1|accessdate=25 January 2010}}</ref> This morphological form was first published as "var. ''dichotoma''" by J. A. Mazrimas in a 1976 volume of the ''[[Carnivorous Plant Newsletter]]'', but the publication of that name was invalid under the rules of the [[International Code of Botanical Nomenclature]]. Even though the name is not valid, it is still widely used in cultivation to refer to this ''D. binata'' form.<ref name="Gilbert 1984" /><ref name="Schlauer" /><ref name="Mazrimas 1976">Mazrimas, J. A. 1976. [http://carnivorousplants.org/cpn/articles/CPNv05n1p15.pdf The ''Drosera binata'' complex.] ''[[Carnivorous Plant Newsletter]]'', 5(1): 15.</ref> This was one of many plants used by [[Charles Darwin]] in his investigation of carnivorous plants for his 1875 book ''[[Insectivorous Plants (book)|Insectivorous Plants]]''.<ref name="Gilbert 1984" /><ref name="Darwin">Darwin, C. 1875. [http://darwin-online.org.uk/content/frameset?viewtype=side&itemID=F1217&pageseq=297 ''Insectivorous Plants''.] London: John Murray. pp. 281-282.</ref>

A third described form, often called ''D. binata'' [[form (botany)|f.]] ''multifida'', has even more leaf divisions, bifurcating several times to produce anywhere from eight to 16 or even 30 terminal leaf points.<ref name="Gilbert 1984" /><ref name="Rice 2010" /> This, too, was published by J. A. Mazrimas in the same 1976 volume of the ''Carnivorous Plant Newsletter'' as var. ''multifida'', referring to the description of a 27-point ''D. binata'' found by George Ashley and published in a 1975 volume of the ''Carnivorous Plant Newsletter''.<ref name="Mazrimas 1976" /><ref name="Ashley 1975">Ashley, G. 1975. [http://carnivorousplants.org/cpn/articles/CPNv04n3p48.pdf The search for the 27 point ''Drosera binata''.] ''[[Carnivorous Plant Newsletter]]'', 4(3): 48.</ref> Neither of these names were validly published, but again they remain in use among carnivorous plant growers. A final form, known for producing up to 40 terminal leaf points, is frequently titled f. ''extrema'', another name that has never been validly published but remains in use.<ref name="Gilbert 1984" />This represents  five-fold dichotomy, with some points undergoing the beginnings of a sixth. The variety ''D.b.'' f. ''extrema'' is native to [[Stradbroke Island]] off the coast of [[Brisbane]], Queensland.<ref>{{cite book | last=Slack | first= Adrian | date= 1980 | title= Carnivorous Plants | location= Cambridge, Massachusetts | publisher= Massachusetts Institute of Technology | pages= 152–153 | isbn= 0-262-19186-5 }}</ref>

Two [[cultivar]]s of ''D. binata'' have been named. ''Drosera'' 'Giant' is a particularly large form of the "var. ''dichotoma''" type and was published by [[Peter D'Amato]] in 1998 and registered in 1999. The other, ''Drosera'' 'Marston Dragon', was published by [[Adrian Slack]] in 1986 and registered in 2001.<ref name="Schlauer" />
